doc.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Cecilia, Elvin Jones and jazz education
title: Mass media, jazz audiences and the weakened NEA
summary: Foster doesn't worry about mass media, thinks one in ten people may like jazz, and says the NEA has lost its teeth.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: But I’m not even worried about where that branch of the media goes with it, because I’ve narrowed down my scope. I’m not concerned with mass media. I don’t think jazz is for everyone. I think one in ten people might appreciate jazz, and in that one person, I’ll zero in on. The other nine, I don’t know if there’s any prospects of their becoming jazz-oriented.
Any more than they’re oriented to serious classical music, serious painting, serious dance, serious fiction, or serious anything else.

When you mention serous classical music, you struck another nerve in regard to the National Endowment and other granting organizations. It seems they have been stripped of all their guts in the present day. When I was involved with the National Endowment, substantive grants were given to musicians of merit, jazz musicians who were able to do quite a bit. But since they lost all their teeth, they have no more bite. I don’t even know what if possible can be done as far as grants to musicians.
